blocks.title: Count signs in an unsorted sample
blocks.prompt:
An independent sample records daily call lengths in minutes.

Test whether the population median call length is greater than 40 minutes.

ObservationLength (minutes)
1\(47\)
2\(27\)
3\(43\)
4\(31\)
5\(35\)
6\(57\)
7\(25\)

Count the positive and negative signs.
blocks.hint: A positive sign means a value above the null median, or a positive after-minus-before difference. Choose the tail from the alternative.

Compare each observation with \(40\).

There are \(3\) positive and \(4\) negative signs.

\(B\sim\mathrm{Bin}\left(7,\tfrac{1}{2}\right)\) under the null hypothesis.

sections.title: When can a normal approximation help?
sections.label: Large samples
sections.intro: For a large sign count and a fair null probability, a normal approximation can estimate the tail.

blocks.html: \(B\approx\mathrm N(\tfrac n2,\tfrac n4)\). For \(\mathrm P(B\ge b)\) use \(b-\tfrac12\); for \(\mathrm P(B\le b)\) use \(b+\tfrac12\).

blocks.title: Find a large-sample upper-tail probability
blocks.prompt:
Independent sign comparisons have been made for the sample of call lengths. A plus means the value exceeds the null median.

Test whether the population median call length is greater than 40 minutes.

There are \(40\) usable observations and \(28\) positive signs.

Find the p-value to 4 decimal places using the normal approximation.
blocks.hint: A positive sign means a value above the null median, or a positive after-minus-before difference. Choose the tail from the alternative.
blocks.solution:
The signs are independent.

There are \(28\) positive and \(12\) negative signs.

\(B\sim\mathrm{Bin}\left(40,\tfrac{1}{2}\right)\) under the null hypothesis.

The null distribution has mean \(20\) and variance \(10\).

Use the continuity boundary \(\frac{55}{2}\).

The relevant normal tail \(\mathrm P(Z\ge \frac{\frac{55}{2}-20}{\sqrt{10}})\) gives \(0.0089\).

There is sufficient evidence that the population median call length is greater than 40 minutes.
